opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a split by timescale and by abstraction.

Low-level control is the part that touches physics directly. It runs fast, maybe hundreds of hertz up to a kilohertz, and its job is to turn a target into torques at the joints. The targets might be a joint position, a foot placement, or a body velocity. It has to deal with contact, balance, motor dynamics, and disturbances like someone pushing the robot or the ground being slippery. Classically this was things like PD control, whole-body control, or model predictive control on a simplified model. More recently a lot of it is reinforcement learning policies trained in simulation and transferred to hardware. Either way, the key property is that it's reactive and robust. It doesn't need to know *why* it's walking somewhere; it just needs to not fall over while getting there.

High-level control works on a slower timescale. It decides what the robot should be doing: where to go, which path to take, whether to step over an obstacle or go around it, when to switch from walking to climbing. It reasons more about the task and the environment, using perception, maps, and increasingly language or vision models. Its output is usually a command that the low-level controller can follow, like "move forward at this velocity" or "put your foot here."

What I find interesting is that the boundary isn't fixed. It's really a design choice about the interface. If the interface is very simple, like a velocity command, the high-level planner is easy to build, but you lose expressiveness. The robot can't do very agile or creative things because the low level only knows how to track velocities. If the interface is richer, like full-body motion targets or keyframes, you can do much more, but the low level has to be more capable and the high level has to know more about the body.

Part of the field's progress has been pushing more capability into the low level, so it can handle rough terrain, parkour-style movements, recovery from falls, and so on, without the high level micromanaging. At the same time, there's a trend toward end-to-end learning, where you try to dissolve the boundary altogether and go from pixels to actions. I think that's promising, but in practice the hierarchy is still very useful. It gives you modularity, you can debug each part, and you can reuse a good locomotion controller across many tasks.

So my short answer: low-level control is about the body, and high-level control is about the task. The interesting research question is what language they should speak to each other.

r001.rationale: High-level control is described as deciding what the robot should do, including where to go and how to navigate obstacles.

r002.rationale: Low-level control is described as turning targets into joint torques while handling contact, balance, and disturbances to carry out the motion.

r003.rationale: The response names reinforcement-learning policies as a low-level control approach for locomotion; the surrounding discussion connects them to carrying out locomotion targets.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the division is really about timescales and about what the system is being asked to reason over.

Low-level control is the part that deals with the physics directly. It's running at hundreds or thousands of hertz, it's closing the loop on joint torques, contact forces, balance. Its job is to make the body do what it's told and not fall over while doing it. Whether that's a whole-body controller, a model-predictive controller, or a learned policy outputting joint targets, it's fundamentally about stabilization and tracking. It doesn't need to know why you're walking across the room.

High-level control is where the "why" lives. It's operating at a much slower rate, maybe a few hertz, sometimes slower. It's deciding where to go, which foothold to pick, whether to step over the obstacle or around it, whether to slow down because the terrain looks loose. It's reasoning over perception, over goals, over a longer horizon.

The interesting thing is that the boundary has moved a lot. Classically, high-level produced footstep plans or velocity commands, and low-level turned those into torques. That was clean, but the interface was lossy. The planner had to abstract the dynamics away, and the controller had to trust that the plan was feasible. A lot of failure cases lived in that gap.

With learning-based approaches, the boundary has blurred. You can train a single policy that takes in terrain perception and outputs joint targets directly, which effectively collapses the hierarchy. That works surprisingly well for locomotion, because walking is a fairly repetitive skill. But it tends to break down when you want the robot to do something with longer-horizon structure, like navigation with semantic goals or manipulation while walking. Then you find yourself putting a hierarchy back in, just with different interfaces.

So my honest answer is that the division isn't fundamental. It's an engineering choice about where you put abstraction and where you put feedback. A good decomposition is one where each layer can be robust to what the other gets wrong. The low-level controller should handle the disturbances the planner didn't anticipate, and the high-level layer should be able to replan when the controller can't execute. If you've drawn the line somewhere and neither layer can cover for the other, you've probably drawn it in the wrong place.

r002.rationale: It describes low-level control as converting commands into torques and handling stabilization and tracking so the body executes what it is told.

r003.rationale: The response mentions a learned policy outputting joint targets, but does not identify reinforcement learning or say it realizes a desired gait.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a division between deciding what the robot should do and making that happen physically. High-level control might choose a direction, a target speed, or where to place the next footstep. Low-level control turns those goals into joint commands or torques while keeping the robot balanced and responding to contact with the ground.

They also operate on different timescales. Planning can happen more slowly, but if a foot slips, the robot needs to react immediately. You don’t want every small correction to require a new high-level decision.

The boundary isn’t absolute, though. A footstep planner needs to understand what the body can actually execute, and the low-level controller needs to communicate when a command is becoming infeasible. So the important thing is the interface: what goals you pass down, what feedback you pass up, and whether those two layers work together.

r002.rationale: It says low-level control converts those goals into joint commands or torques and handles balance and ground contact.

r003.rationale: It does not mention reinforcement learning as a way to implement low-level control or realize a desired gait.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the division in terms of what the robot should do versus how it executes that motion. The high-level controller sets goals—where to go, which direction to move, or what speed to maintain. The low-level controller turns those goals into coordinated joint actions while maintaining balance and responding to contact with the ground.

But the boundary isn’t fixed. A high-level controller might specify footsteps, or it might just provide a desired velocity and let the low-level controller choose the stepping pattern. The important thing is that the two levels have a useful interface: the high level should ask for motions the robot can actually execute, and the low level should provide feedback when those requests need to change.
